subject: TTFT & streaming SLO follow-up — Time-to-first-token targets and chunk cadence
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwoodinference.com>
To: Alice Ng <alice@timestreamlabs.com>, Bob Carter <bob.carter@timestreamlabs.com>
Cc: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwoodinference.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Sat, 18 Jul 2026 14:02:00 -0700
Subject: TTFT & streaming SLO follow-up — initial summary and next steps

Hi Alice / Bob —

Thanks again for the demo and the deep-dive today. Per our conversation, I wanted to summarize the performance and streaming requirements you shared and propose next steps so we can size a test and scope any SLA language for the deal.

Quick summary of requirements you highlighted:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): target p95 <= 250 ms from request acceptance (aiming for 150–200 ms ideally) for short prompts (~128–512 tokens).
- Streaming delivery: browser UI expects incremental partials (SSE or WebSocket) with chunk cadence between 50–250 ms (goal: ~100 ms cadence for snappy UX).
- Throughput / concurrency: steady-state ~50 req/s, burst up to 200 req/s; peak concurrent streams ~30–40.
- Model context: 2k token windows for user+system; some requests will use longer context (4k) and can accept slightly higher TTFT.
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 breakdown and a definition for when fallback to non-streaming or lower-fidelity model is allowed.

Proposed next steps:
1) Engineering perf run: Redwood runs a targeted perf test with a sample workload (we'll emulate your concurrency and chunk cadence) and share p50/p95/p99 TTFT and end-to-end streaming latency.
2) Canary & config: discuss dedicated capacity (reserved pool) vs hosted with routing; Vivek will recommend quantization/model variants to hit the TTFT targets.
3) Contract language: if the perf run meets agreed p95 TTFT and streaming cadence, we'll add a perf SLA to the deal (we can draft language).
4) Artifacts: please share a sample of production throughput patterns (per-minute QPS), preferred endpoints (SSE vs WS), and any network egress constraints.

Attachments: if you have a network diagram or proxy/load-balancer details, please send — that helps us tune chunk sizes and TCP/HTTP settings.

Would love confirmation on the numbers above (especially p95 TTFT and peak concurrency). I can schedule the perf run as early as next week if you can provide the usage profile.

Thanks,
Marissa

Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming SLO follow-up — initial summary and next steps

Marissa —

This looks right, thanks for the clear recap. A couple clarifications from our side: 
- p95 TTFT target: firm requirement is <= 250 ms at peak concurrency (we'd prefer 150–200 ms but we can be flexible if the perf run demonstrates consistency).
- Streaming cadence: 100–200 ms is our sweet spot. Anything slower than ~300 ms feels laggy to users.
- Concurrency: peak concurrent streams will be ~40 during spikes; steady concurrency ~10–15.
- Fallback behavior: if streaming can't meet cadence we need a deterministic fallback that doesn't break the UI (e.g., switch to chunked non-streaming but preserve partials).

Sending two attachments: network_diagram.pdf and security_questionnaire.xlsx (redacted where appropriate). We'll also attach a short sample of production QPS distribution in the next email.

Can you include Vivek and the infra team in the perf run planning? We'd like to observe one run and get the raw logs for p95 calculations.

Thanks — Alice
Alice Ng

Subject: Re: TTFT & streaming SLO follow-up — initial summary and next steps

Hi all —

Thanks for the detailed requirements — quick technical notes from the infra/serving side: 

1) TTFT drivers and mitigation options:
   - Model size & chunking: smaller decoder-only variants and aggressive KV cache reuse will reduce TTFT. For your 2k context, we can target p95 ~150–220 ms with a trimmed model and optimized kernels.
   - Quantization: int4/QLoRa options can help reduce per-token latency; we'll test 4-bit pathing during the perf run.
   - Dedicated capacity: reserving GPU pools significantly reduces jitter; recommend a dedicated pool for your latency-sensitive streams.

2) Streaming (SSE vs WebSocket):
   - SSE: simpler for browser clients and works well with existing HTTP infra; server push fits our chunked flush model.
   - WebSocket: lower overhead for long-lived connections and bi-directional control messages (e.g., edit/cancel).
   - Tradeoffs: SSE is easier with existing load balancers; WS needs sticky routing or connection-aware routing. Both can meet the cadence requirement if we tune batching and flush thresholds.

3) Chunk cadence & network tuning:
   - Cadence target: we'll aim for 80–150 ms cadence during perf tests. We recommend emitting smaller token deltas frequently (e.g., every 40–100 tokens or every 80–150 ms), with an upper bound of 250 ms so UI stays responsive.
   - TCP/TLS buffers: we'll provide recommended keepalive and Nagle settings to avoid coalescing latency.

4) Test plan ask:
   - Can you provide a representative traffic trace (1 week preferred) and a sample payload set (short, medium, long contexts)?
   - We'll run 3 rounds: baseline (hosted), quantized variant, dedicated-reserved pool. We'll produce p50/p95/p99 TTFT, per-chunk latency distribution, and CPU/GPU utilization.

I'll draft a short perf plan and will attach it (perf_plan.md). If the perf results look good we can propose a short SLA clause with guarded thresholds and allowed maintenance windows.

Vivek
Senior Infra Engineer — Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference
